name: Threat Modeling Conventions
description: This module defines the naming, formatting, and structural style conventions to follow whenever writing, implementing, or reviewing threat modeling code or output, so results stay consistent with the existing threat modeling style guide.
content:
This module defines the naming, formatting, and structural style conventions to follow whenever writing, implementing, or reviewing threat modeling code or output, so results stay consistent with the existing threat modeling style guide.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. When threat modeling guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
2. Check that threat modeling terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
3. Prefer explicit, readable threat modeling solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
4. When multiple threat modeling strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
5. Measure before optimizing any threat modeling bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
6. Before starting threat modeling work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
7. Re-check edge cases relevant to threat modeling (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
8. When threat modeling decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
9. Keep threat modeling changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
10. Document any non-obvious threat modeling decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
11. State assumptions about threat modeling explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of threat modeling correctness.
- Avoid introducing new threat modeling abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not apply generic threat modeling advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Do not silently drop threat modeling edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.

CLOSING NOTE
When in doubt, prefer clarity and explicit reasoning about threat modeling over a shortcut that saves a few lines but hides intent.
